variants.title: Build a leakage-resistant feature set
variants.context: pandas will execute any transformation, but it cannot tell you that a feature leaked the future. The four steps are to define prediction time, split by the deployment boundary, fit transformation state on training rows once, then apply and verify the frozen contract on evaluation and serving rows.
variants.prompt: A churn model will score customers the business has never seen before. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Partition by customer so no customer's rows appear on both sides of the boundary.
State the entity, target, decision time, prediction horizon, and which facts are observable before that decision.
Transform the evaluation and serving rows with the same state, ordered columns, dtypes, and edge-case behavior.
Learn imputation values, category vocabularies, and scaling statistics from the training rows only.

variants.hint: The deployment boundary has to be named before it can be enforced.
variants.explanation: Frame, separate, learn, reproduce. A random row split would put the same customer on both sides and inflate the held-out score.

variants.title: Build a leakage-resistant feature set
variants.context: pandas will execute any transformation, but it cannot tell you that a feature leaked the future. The four steps are to define prediction time, split by the deployment boundary, fit transformation state on training rows once, then apply and verify the frozen contract on evaluation and serving rows.
variants.prompt: A demand model is backtested on forward-moving periods. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Fit the scaling and encoding state on each training period alone.
Cut forward-time partitions so every evaluation period follows its training period.
Apply that state unchanged to the following period and compare the columns, dtypes, and null behavior.
Fix the decision time for each prediction and the horizon it forecasts.

variants.hint: Which partition is allowed to contribute a statistic to the next one?
variants.explanation: In a forward backtest the state is refitted per period, and applying a later period's statistics backwards is the leak the design exists to prevent.

variants.title: Build a leakage-resistant feature set
variants.context: pandas will execute any transformation, but it cannot tell you that a feature leaked the future. The four steps are to define prediction time, split by the deployment boundary, fit transformation state on training rows once, then apply and verify the frozen contract on evaluation and serving rows.
variants.prompt: The team wants evidence that offline and serving transformations agree. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the fitted transformation state as a versioned artifact rather than recomputing it per environment.
Write down the prediction time and the observable facts the contract promises at that moment.
Run both the training and serving code over the shared fixture and compare ordered columns, dtypes, and values.
Hold out the rows that the shared fixture will use as its evaluation and adversarial cases.

variants.hint: Parity is proven by running both paths, not by reading both implementations.
variants.explanation: Shared fixtures on normal and adversarial rows are the evidence that two code paths implement one contract.

variants.title: Make a window point backward
variants.context: Time-series correctness starts with an explicit clock. Event time is when something happened and ingestion time is when the system observed it, so late arrivals make current row order unsafe. Parse timestamps deliberately, sort by entity and event time before shift or rolling operations, end windows before the prediction event, record a late-data policy, and backtest with forward-moving periods.
variants.prompt: A 7-day rolling purchase count is built per customer from an events table. Put the steps in order.

items.text: End each window before its own prediction event so the current outcome cannot enter its own feature.
Backtest with forward-moving periods that resemble deployment.
Sort by customer and event time so row order reflects the clock rather than arrival.
Record the late-data and correction policy instead of silently rebuilding history.
Parse the timestamp column deliberately and normalize its time zones.

variants.hint: What does the frame's current row order actually prove?
variants.explanation: Parse, sort, bound, document, backtest. A rolling operation trusts row order, so sorting by entity and event time is a precondition, not a style choice.

variants.title: Make a window point backward
variants.context: Time-series correctness starts with an explicit clock. Event time is when something happened and ingestion time is when the system observed it, so late arrivals make current row order unsafe. Parse timestamps deliberately, sort by entity and event time before shift or rolling operations, end windows before the prediction event, record a late-data policy, and backtest with forward-moving periods.
variants.prompt: Events arrive from two regions in local time and some are delivered hours late. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Sort within each entity by the normalized event time rather than by ingestion order.
Write down whether a late record updates the prior value or is dropped with a measured reason.
Close each window before the prediction event so a late arrival cannot be counted into its own row.
Replay forward-moving periods to confirm the backtest matches what deployment would have produced.
Parse both regions' timestamps and normalize them to one time zone before comparing them.

variants.hint: Two clocks disagree here: when it happened and when it landed.
variants.explanation: Normalizing time zones first is what makes the sort meaningful, and the late-data policy is what makes corrections reproducible.

variants.title: Make a window point backward
variants.context: Time-series correctness starts with an explicit clock. Event time is when something happened and ingestion time is when the system observed it, so late arrivals make current row order unsafe. Parse timestamps deliberately, sort by entity and event time before shift or rolling operations, end windows before the prediction event, record a late-data policy, and backtest with forward-moving periods.
variants.prompt: A shift-based previous-value feature is wrong because the frame arrived in ingestion order. Put the steps in order for the fix.

items.text: Sort by entity and event time so shift moves along the real timeline.
Verify the shifted value comes strictly from before the prediction event.
Document how a correction to an earlier event should be replayed.
Confirm the event-time column parses correctly and carries no mixed time zones.
Re-run the forward-moving backtest to confirm the repaired feature.

variants.hint: shift moves along row order, whatever that order happens to be.
variants.explanation: shift, rolling, and expanding operations all read the current row order, so an unsorted frame silently produces future-looking values.

variants.title: Budget the frame
variants.context: memory_usage(deep=True) measures the current frame, not the peak of a transformation. A teaching envelope budgets 8 bytes per numeric element and 8 bytes plus the average UTF-8 payload per text element, then multiplies the payload by a peak multiplier to account for sorts, merges, casts, indexes, and intermediate arrays.
variants.prompt: A frame has 30 numeric columns and 5 text columns whose values average 24 UTF-8 bytes. Using 8 bytes per numeric element and 8 bytes plus the payload per text element, how many bytes does one row cost?
variants.hint: Each text element carries a pointer as well as its characters.
variants.explanation: Per-row cost is the numeric width plus the text width, and the text width includes the fixed overhead per element as well as the payload.

mistakes.feedback: Counted only the numeric columns and ignored the text ones.
Left out the 8-byte overhead on each text element and counted the payload alone.

variants.title: Budget the frame
variants.context: memory_usage(deep=True) measures the current frame, not the peak of a transformation. A teaching envelope budgets 8 bytes per numeric element and 8 bytes plus the average UTF-8 payload per text element, then multiplies the payload by a peak multiplier to account for sorts, merges, casts, indexes, and intermediate arrays.
variants.prompt: A frame's visible payload is 6 gigabytes and the transformation is estimated to need a peak multiplier of 2.5. What is the estimated peak?
variants.hint: The multiplier scales the payload rather than being added to it.
variants.explanation: Sorts, merges, casts, and intermediate arrays can require multiples of the visible payload, which is why the peak is the quantity to plan against.

mistakes.feedback: Added the multiplier to the payload instead of multiplying by it.
Divided the payload by the multiplier instead of multiplying.

variants.title: Budget the frame
variants.context: memory_usage(deep=True) measures the current frame, not the peak of a transformation. A teaching envelope budgets 8 bytes per numeric element and 8 bytes plus the average UTF-8 payload per text element, then multiplies the payload by a peak multiplier to account for sorts, merges, casts, indexes, and intermediate arrays.
variants.prompt: A machine has 20 gigabytes available. A frame's payload is 4.5 gigabytes and the planned transformation has a peak multiplier of 3. How much headroom remains at the peak?
variants.hint: Compare the machine against the peak, not against the resting frame.
variants.explanation: Headroom is available memory minus the estimated peak, so planning against the visible payload alone is how a job fails partway through.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the peak itself rather than the memory left over at that peak.
Subtracted only the visible payload and ignored the temporary copies.

variants.title: Name the join and its guard
variants.context: A merge is model logic because it can change the statistical weight of the training set. A dimension lookup attaches one record per example and must reject duplicate dimension keys. A point-in-time join picks the latest fact available before the prediction with explicit event-time ordering and a freshness policy. A relationship expansion is many to many and has to be aggregated or weighted intentionally.
variants.prompt: Each order should gain one product record, but after the merge the order count rose by 4 percent. What is the shape and the guard?
options: A point-in-time join, guarded by ordering the product table by event time before merging.
A relationship expansion, guarded by aggregating the extra rows back down after the merge.
A dimension lookup, guarded by validating many-to-one and rejecting duplicate product keys.
optionFeedback: There is no second clock in this lookup, so event-time ordering does not address a duplicated key.
Treating an accidental multiplication as an intended expansion hides the broken dimension table.
Correct: a duplicated dimension key is what multiplies rows, and the cardinality assertion catches it at the merge.
variants.hint: How many dimension rows was each order supposed to match?
variants.explanation: A merge can change the statistical weight of the training set, so the expected cardinality is asserted rather than assumed.

variants.title: Name the join and its guard
variants.context: A merge is model logic because it can change the statistical weight of the training set. A dimension lookup attaches one record per example and must reject duplicate dimension keys. A point-in-time join picks the latest fact available before the prediction with explicit event-time ordering and a freshness policy. A relationship expansion is many to many and has to be aggregated or weighted intentionally.
variants.prompt: Each application should gain the applicant's most recent credit score as known at decision time. What is the shape and the guard?
options: A point-in-time join, guarded by explicit event-time ordering and a freshness policy.
A dimension lookup, guarded by validating many-to-one against the applicant table.
A relationship expansion, guarded by weighting each score by how recent it is.
optionFeedback: Correct: the correct row depends on the decision time, so ordering and a staleness rule are what the merge needs.
An applicant has many scores over time, so a one-to-one dimension assertion would fail or pick an arbitrary row.
Expanding to every historical score and reweighting them answers a different question than latest known fact.
variants.hint: Which fact is correct depends on when you ask.
variants.explanation: A point-in-time join selects the latest fact available before prediction, which needs event-time ordering and a declared freshness policy.

variants.title: Name the join and its guard
variants.context: A merge is model logic because it can change the statistical weight of the training set. A dimension lookup attaches one record per example and must reject duplicate dimension keys. A point-in-time join picks the latest fact available before the prediction with explicit event-time ordering and a freshness policy. A relationship expansion is many to many and has to be aggregated or weighted intentionally.
variants.prompt: Customers belong to several marketing segments, and joining segments tripled the training rows. The relationship is genuinely many to many. What should be done?
options: Treat it as a relationship expansion and aggregate or weight it intentionally before training.
Add a many-to-one validation so the merge fails until the segment table is deduplicated.
Keep the expanded rows as they are, since every customer-segment pair is a real observation.
optionFeedback: Correct: the expansion is legitimate, so the decision is how it should count, not whether to allow it.
The data really is many to many, so asserting many-to-one would reject a correct table.
Leaving it unweighted silently gives multi-segment customers three times the influence on the model.
variants.hint: The row count changed for a real reason, but what does that do to each customer's weight?
variants.explanation: A many-to-many merge changes the statistical weight of the training set, so aggregation or weighting is a modeling decision to make deliberately.

variants.title: Hold the runtime contract
variants.context: pandas 3 made Copy-on-Write the default, so code that relied on chained assignment or accidental view mutation needs explicit .loc updates and version-specific tests. Pin the runtime, avoid repeated concatenation in a loop, preserve stable row identifiers through filters and joins, and fail on unexpected schema drift rather than coercing everything to strings.
variants.prompt: A feature job appends each day's partition with a concatenation inside the loop, and it slows sharply as the number of days grows. What is the fix?
options: Collect the partitions in a list and concatenate them once at the end.
Reserve the full frame up front and assign each day's rows into it by position.
Add worker processes so the repeated concatenations run in parallel.
optionFeedback: Correct: repeated concatenation rebuilds the whole frame each iteration, and one concatenation at the end does not.
Positional assignment into a preallocated frame is fragile and does not address the repeated copying that causes the slowdown.
Parallelism adds serialization and inter-process copies on top of work that is already quadratic.
variants.hint: What is being rebuilt on every pass through the loop?
variants.explanation: Avoid repeated concatenation in a loop. Collect the partitions and concatenate once so the frame is built a single time.

variants.title: Hold the runtime contract
variants.context: pandas 3 made Copy-on-Write the default, so code that relied on chained assignment or accidental view mutation needs explicit .loc updates and version-specific tests. Pin the runtime, avoid repeated concatenation in a loop, preserve stable row identifiers through filters and joins, and fail on unexpected schema drift rather than coercing everything to strings.
variants.prompt: After an upgrade to pandas 3, a step that used to update the frame through a chained assignment now leaves it unchanged. What should the team do?
options: Copy the frame before every mutation so the chained assignment writes to a fresh object.
Rewrite the update as an explicit .loc assignment and add version-specific tests.
Suppress the assignment warnings globally so the upgraded code runs quietly.
optionFeedback: Copying first does not make a chained assignment reach the original frame, and it multiplies memory use.
Correct: Copy-on-Write is the default in pandas 3, so the update has to be written explicitly and pinned by a test.
Silencing warnings globally hides the exact signal that would have found this and the next occurrence.
variants.hint: Which pandas version's behavior is the code assuming?
variants.explanation: Pin the runtime, write updates explicitly with .loc, and assert output columns, dtypes, null behavior, and representative values across versions.

variants.title: Hold the runtime contract
variants.context: pandas 3 made Copy-on-Write the default, so code that relied on chained assignment or accidental view mutation needs explicit .loc updates and version-specific tests. Pin the runtime, avoid repeated concatenation in a loop, preserve stable row identifiers through filters and joins, and fail on unexpected schema drift rather than coercing everything to strings.
variants.prompt: An upstream producer starts sending a numeric column with occasional text values, and the loader quietly casts the whole column to strings. What is the right response?
options: Keep the coercion and cast back to numeric downstream where the values are used.
Cast the column to a nullable numeric type so the text values become nulls.
Fail on the unexpected schema drift instead of coercing the column.
optionFeedback: Casting back later spreads the problem across the codebase and still loses the values that will not parse.
Turning unexplained text into nulls discards the evidence of the producer regression.
Correct: a silent dtype change alters every downstream feature, so the job should stop and surface it.
variants.hint: Which response leaves the producer change visible?
variants.explanation: Fail on unexpected schema drift rather than coercing everything to strings, because a dtype that changes between environments changes the model's inputs.
